name: Question 3
problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14114783/assets/4121d975786de30f34e493e7ac49e5cdc8e66621e800321008ba4ba501fb818f.png)

If $D$ is the finite region enclosed by the curves $y=-{x}^{2},$ and $y=-1,$ as shown above, then ${∬}_{D}({x}^{2}y-3x)\,dA=$
worked_solution:
First, let's represent $D$ as a type I region. 

- To determine the $x$-limits, we need to find the $x$-coordinates of the points at which the curves intersect. So, we set the following equation and solve it for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-{x}^{2} & =-1 \\ {x}^{2} & =1 \\ x & =\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

So, $x$-limits are 
$-1\le x\le 1.$

- To determine the lower and upper functions, we draw a vertical arrow through the region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14114783/assets/ef6450f795d0edea8a3217e28d7f1a966d5b1c62f9241826213de0485af5f860.png)

As a result, we get

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,-1\le x\le 1,\,-1\le y\le -{x}^{2}}.
$$

Therefore, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}({x}^{2}y-3x)\,dA & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{-1}^{-{x}^{2}}({x}^{2}y-3x)\,dy\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

If D is the finite region enclosed by the curves y=−x2, and y=−1, as shown above, then ∬D(x2y−3x)dA=

a
∫01∫−1−x2(x2y−3x)dydx
b
∫−11∫−1−x2(x2y−3x)dydx
c
∫−x2−1∫01(x2y−3x)dydx
d
∫−1−x2∫−11(x2y−3x)dydx
e
∫−11∫−x2−1(x2y−3x)dydx
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, let's represent D as a type I region.

  • To determine the x-limits, we need to find the x-coordinates of the points at which the curves intersect. So, we set the following equation and solve it for x: −x2=−1x2=1x=±1 So, x-limits are −1≤x≤1.

  • To determine the lower and upper functions, we draw a vertical arrow through the region.

As a result, we get

D={(x,y):−1≤x≤1,−1≤y≤−x2}.

Therefore, we can express the integral as follows:

∬D(x2y−3x)dA=∫−11∫−1−x2(x2y−3x)dydx
